summary: Describes how to proxy UDP through HTTP, much as the HTTP CONNECT method proxies TCP. It defines a protocol letting an HTTP client create a tunnel for UDP traffic through an HTTP server acting as a proxy. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A helper at the front desk can pass your regular letters on. Now they can also pass along quick postcards, sending UDP messages for you through the web connection.

subtitle: How an HTTP client asks a proxy to carry UDP packets, much as CONNECT carries TCP.

tldr.problem: HTTP has a CONNECT method for tunneling TCP through a proxy, but before this RFC it had no method for UDP traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends a request with the connect-udp upgrade token to a URL built from a URI Template with target_host and target_port. If it succeeds, the proxy opens a UDP socket to the target and converts HTTP Datagrams to UDP packets and back.
tldr.outcome: Every HTTP version is supported, and the tunnel can carry protocols such as QUIC. The proxy must be protected against abuse, so use should be restricted to authenticated users.

today: RFC 9298 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2022. It is updated by RFC 9484 and RFC 9931, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: Proxying UDP over HTTP
sections.content:
The HTTP CONNECT method creates a TCP tunnel through a proxy, but there was no equivalent for UDP. RFC 9298 describes a protocol for tunneling UDP to a server acting as a UDP proxy over HTTP. Such tunnels are commonly used to create an end-to-end virtual connection that is then secured with QUIC or another protocol running over UDP.

Unlike CONNECT, the proxy is identified by an absolute URL that contains the traffic's destination. Clients build these URLs from a URI Template. The protocol works with every HTTP version by using HTTP Datagrams (RFC 9297). HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 use Extended CONNECT, and HTTP/1.x uses HTTP Upgrade.
sections.plainLanguage: There was already a way to send phone-call-style traffic through a helper. This adds a way to send quick postcard-style traffic through a helper too.

sections.title: Client Configuration with URI Templates
sections.content:
A client is configured with a URI Template (RFC 6570) that has the variables target_host and target_port. One example from the RFC is https://example.org/.well-known/masque/udp/{target_host}/{target_port}/.

The template MUST be level 3 or lower and in absolute form with non-empty scheme, authority and path. The path MUST start with a slash, and all variables MUST be in the path or query. It MUST NOT contain non-ASCII characters. It MUST NOT use Reserved, Fragment, Dot-Prefix Label, Slash-Prefix Path Segment or Semicolon-Prefix Path-Style Parameter expansion. A client that finds a violation MUST reject the configuration and abort without sending the request.

Some clients can only configure a proxy host and port. They MAY use the default template https://$PROXY_HOST:$PROXY_PORT/.well-known/masque/udp/{target_host}/{target_port}/, and proxies that need to interoperate with them SHOULD offer service at that location.
sections.plainLanguage: The client has a fill-in-the-blanks address. It writes the target's name and door number into the blanks to say where the postcards should go.

sections.title: Setting Up the Tunnel
sections.content:
The RFC defines the connect-udp HTTP upgrade token. The target is given by the template variables: target_host can be a DNS name, an IPv6 literal or an IPv4 literal, and target_port MUST be an integer from 1 to 65535. In an IPv6 literal the colons MUST be percent-encoded, so 2001:db8::42 becomes 2001%3Adb8%3A%3A42. Scoped zone identifiers are not supported.

With HTTP/1.1, the request uses the GET method with a Host header, Connection: Upgrade and Upgrade: connect-udp. Success is a 101 (Switching Protocols) response with matching Connection and Upgrade headers. With HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, the request is an Extended CONNECT with :method set to CONNECT and :protocol set to connect-udp, and success is any 2xx status. In both cases the response must also start the Capsule Protocol, and neither request nor successful response carries message content.

An HTTP intermediary forwards the request on to another server. Otherwise the recipient acts as the UDP proxy: it decodes the variables and opens a UDP socket to the target. UDP is connectionless, so the proxy cannot know whether the target is reachable and replies without waiting for a packet. If the target is a DNS name, the proxy MUST resolve it before replying and MUST reject the request on error, and it SHOULD report details with a Proxy-Status header field.
sections.plainLanguage: The client knocks and says "please open a postcard tunnel to this address". The helper checks the address and, if all is well, says yes without waiting to hear whether anyone is home.

sections.title: Context IDs and Datagram Format
sections.content:
Every HTTP Datagram on a UDP proxying stream starts with a Context ID, a variable-length integer. Context IDs are 62-bit values. Zero is reserved for UDP payloads. Non-zero even values are allocated by the client and odd values by the proxy, which avoids the need for synchronization. This leaves room for future extensions to carry other kinds of data on the same tunnel; the RFC does not define how Context IDs are registered.

The datagram payload is the Context ID followed by the UDP Proxying Payload. With Context ID zero, the payload is the unmodified data octets of a UDP packet, and it MUST NOT be longer than 65527 bytes. A receiver that gets a longer one MUST abort the stream. A datagram with an unknown Context ID is either dropped silently or buffered for about a round trip. The same choice applies to a datagram that arrives before its request, and receivers that buffer SHOULD apply buffering limits.

A client MAY start sending datagrams before it receives the response, but they may be ignored if the request fails or the proxy chooses not to buffer them.
sections.plainLanguage: Each postcard gets a small number stamp on the front. Stamp zero means an ordinary UDP postcard. Other numbers are saved for future special kinds of mail.

sections.title: Proxy Behavior and Performance
sections.content:
The socket's lifetime is tied to the request stream. The proxy MUST keep the socket open while the stream is open, and MUST close the stream if the operating system says the socket is no longer usable, for instance after an ICMP Destination Unreachable message. A proxy MAY close idle sockets, but SHOULD NOT use an idle period lower than two minutes. If the proxy uses an unconnected socket, it MUST check the source address and port of received packets and discard mismatches.

The proxy MUST NOT introduce IP fragmentation, and in IPv4 it MUST set the Don't Fragment bit if possible. Oversized datagrams are silently dropped. With HTTP/3 DATAGRAM frames, a UDP payload that does not fit SHOULD be dropped and an ICMP Packet Too Big message sent to the target.

For performance, proxies SHOULD NOT queue packets to increase batching, since bursts can cause correlated loss. Proxied traffic that uses its own congestion control sits under at least two nested controllers, and the HTTP connection MUST NOT disable congestion control unless it knows with absolute certainty that the inner traffic is controlled. Because TCP-based HTTP would nest two loss-recovery mechanisms, UDP proxying SHOULD be performed over HTTP/3. A proxy MUST set the ECN bits to Not-ECT on packets it sends to the target.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper keeps the tunnel open as long as you do, throws away postcards that are too big, and does not pile postcards up and send them all at once.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Letting arbitrary clients tunnel to arbitrary targets is risky because bad actors could send traffic that is attributed to the proxy. Servers that support UDP proxying ought to restrict it to authenticated users.

Some software trusts requests by source IP address, such as accepting configuration changes from 127.0.0.1. Proxied traffic arrives with the proxy's address, so clients could gain privileges they should not have. To prevent this, a proxy should refuse requests to vulnerable targets such as its own addresses, localhost, and link-local, multicast and broadcast addresses, and it can use the destination_ip_prohibited Proxy Error Type.

The RFC also compares UDP proxies with TCP CONNECT proxies as tools for denial-of-service attacks. A TCP proxy stops sending when the target stops replying, but UDP has no shared state, so a UDP proxy could keep sending data to a flooded target.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper who will send mail anywhere can be tricked into sending bad mail. So only people who show ID should get to use the helper, and some doors, like the helper's own, stay off limits.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered connect-udp in the HTTP Upgrade Tokens registry, with the description Proxying of UDP Payloads. It also registered masque in the Well-Known URIs registry, with status permanent. The registration covers all resources under the path prefix /.well-known/masque/udp/.
sections.plainLanguage: The new keyword and the special web address folder were written into the official lists so nobody else uses them for something different.
